text.p: Woolwich Plc shares came bumped back down to earth on Tuesday, the second day of stock market trading in the former mutually-owned mortgage lender turned bank.

Under pressure from the outset after a disappointing response by investment institutions in an auction of stock organised by Woolwich's broker BZW, the stock was down 32.5p at 301.5 by 1444 GMT in heavy trade of 17.8 million shares.
Woolwich said investment funds had pitched their offers at an average 315.35p in the first of a series of auctions of Woolwich shares, a five percent discount to Monday's closing price of 334p.
As with other recent demutualising building societies, the auction was designed to allow institutions such as pension funds to scoop up parcels of stock sold by former Woolwich members.

Today's share price decline came as a disappointment to any new shareholders who had expected to be able to sell out quickly at Monday's inflated levels. Woolwich members enjoyed an average windfall of 2,200 stg ($3,700) at yesterday's close.

Yet the share price retreat was no surprise to market professionsla after the stock's storming market debut, which saw it quoted at a far higher-than-expected 370p at one stage -- valuing the company at around 5.5 billion pounds.
Analysts said Woolwich shares still looked over-priced, even after Tuesday's fall, and were trading on a higher multiple to earnings than rivals in the bank sector.
"If you look at the stock's rating against fundamentals, it still looks too expensive," said one analyst at a leading securities house.

A trader at another brokerage said the stock should be valued well below Tuesday's levels, though speculation that Woolwich could be the target of a takeover bid, as the bank sector consolidates, could underpin the shares.
"We don't see any short-term support above about 270p," the trader said, "but having said that, bid rumours will persist."
Other analysts have valued the stock at as low as 250p.

Dealers said the stock had reached an artificially high level on Monday as market-makers had driven up the price to attract small, retail sellers and to avoid being caught short of stock by potentially strong demand from institutions.

The fall in Woolwich also weighed on other former building societies turned banks. Shares in Abbey National Plc tumbled 32p to 844.5 by 1449 GMT, Halifax Plc was down 6p at 763.5 and Alliance & Leicester Plc slipped 1/2p to 612.5.
Like the Halifax and Alliance & Leicester, Woolwich is poised to join the FTSE 100 index but not until the index is next rejigged in September.
A total of 370 million shares are to be sold through the auction process, representing the 23 percent of the company's capital pre-sold by Woolwich members. ($ = 0.594 British Pounds)
